list.listitem: Suspect acute pancreatitis in patients with acute upper abdominal or back pain. C
Order hepatic transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, serum lipase, and amylase (former is more specific for pancreatitis). C
Clinical rules have been developed and validated that help predict prognosis. The best known are the Ranson, Glasgow (Imrie), and BALI scores (see ). B
Enteral nutrition is more effective and safer than parenteral nutrition. B
Antibiotics are only indicated for infected necrotic pancreatitis and should not be used prophylactically. B
Surgery is recommended for patients with gallstone pancreatitis, unstable infected necrosis, and persistent or enlarging pseudocyst. C

background.definition: Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas, most often caused by gallstones or alcohol use.

list.listitem: Acute pancreatitis: 43.8 cases per 100,000 adults.
255,130 hospital admissions each year.

Gallstones (especially stone 5 mm or less) and excessive alcohol use are the most common identified causes. In a series of 7456 admissions for a first episode of acute pancreatitis, the cause was biliary in 28%, alcohol in 19%, and idiopathic in 36%.

Drugs (eg, azathioprine, thiazides, estrogens, sulindac, tetracycline, valproic acid, furosemide, octreotide, methyldopa, estrogens, 6-mercaptopurine, pentamidine, 5-aminosalicylic acid, and corticosteroids).
Hypertriglyceridemia.
Following endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).
Hypercalcemia.
Trauma or postoperative.
Duct obstruction from tumor.
Scorpion envenemation from certain species.
Inappropriate activation of trypsinogen to trypsin, which is the key enzyme in activation of pancreatic zymogens, and a lack of prompt elimination of trypsin inside the pancreas.
Digestive enzymes cause pancreatic injury and inflammatory response.
Octreotide, somatostatin, and possibly NSAIDs (indomethacin and diclofenac) may reduce the risk of acute pancreatitis following ERCP. B
Treat alcohol use disorders. C

Fibrates are recommended to lower triglycerides in patients with hypertriglyceridemia. Statins are associated with a decreased risk of pancreatitis in patients with normal or mildly elevated triglycerides.

Olezarsen is a novel drug that in a randomized trial of patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome reduced the likelihood of acute pancreatitis by lowering triglyceride levels (1 vs 11 episodes, RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.66). A larger trial found that it significantly lowered the risk of acute pancreatitis in persons with triglyceride > 500 mg/dl (1 vs 6 episodes per 100 person-years, NNT = 20). A third small trial evaluated plozasiran in the same population with similar results.B
In high-risk patients, a single dose of rectal indomethacin may prevent post-ERCP pancreatitis (NNT = 13). B
Aggressive hydration with Lactated Ringer's can prevent post ERCP pancreatitis. B

Diagnosis requires two of the following three findings: 1. Abdominal pain (acute onset, severe, persistent, epigastric possibly radiating to back).2. Serum lipase (or amylase) elevated to at least three times the upper limit of normal.3. Findings characteristic of acute pancreatitis on CT with contrast, MRI or ultrasound.
Order amylase, lipase, CBC, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, C-reactive protein, and liver function studies to determine etiology and prognosis. C
Order ultrasound as the initial study for suspected gallstone pancreatitis, and CT (with possible aspiration) for patients with severe acute pancreatitis. C
Consider MR cholangiography if biliary, pancreatic, or common duct stones are suspected. C
For differential diagnosis see topic on Abdominal pain (adult).

Patients with acute pancreatitis typically present with upper abdominal pain, often radiating to the back, and accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Pain typically begins fairly suddenly and is severe; it may be improved in supine position.
Ask about a history of gallstones, excessive use of alcohol, certain drugs as previously mentioned, trauma, and hypertriglyceridemia to determine the cause.
Consider a pancreatic tumor as a cause in patients over 40 years old if no apparent etiology is found.

On examination, patients may be febrile and tachycardic with abdominal tenderness, guarding, and distension. Bowel sounds are typically hypoactive. Diaphragmatic irritation may lead to pleuritic pain or dyspnea; duct obstruction may lead to jaundice in a minority of patients. Patients with severe disease may be hemodynamically unstable, diaphoretic, and have diminished level of consciousness.
Severe necrotizing pancreatitis can cause a reddish brown discoloration in the flank(s) due to extravasation of blood or pancreatic exudate (Grey–Turner sign).
When pancreatitis is suspected clinically, order serum amylase and lipase. Elevation 3 times above the upper limit of normal in the absence of renal failure strongly suggests acute pancreatitis.
Trending amylase and lipase is not recommended as it does not coorelate to severity or prognosis and should not be used to make clinical decisions.

Order alkaline phosphatase and hepatic transaminases to distinguish gallstone pancreatitis from other causes. The combination of elevated AST, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin is strong evidence for cholelithiasis as the cause.
An elevated lipase:amylase ratio increases the likelihood of alcoholic pancreatitis.
Also order triglycerides and calcium to look for etiology, and electrolytes, BUN, serum creatinine, glucose, C-reactive protein, LDH, and CBC to assess severity (along with calcium level).
Risk stratify patients to assess need for more intensive monitoring.
Ultrasound is recommended as the initial imaging study, primarily to detect cholelithiasis. It is of limited value for detecting complications or assessing severity.

CT scan is recommended for patients with severe pancreatitis, evidence of organ failure, and those not improving after 48 hours to determine if there is necrotic pancreas, pseudocyst, or abscess. If found, CT-guided needle aspiration can identify pathogen for culture and sensitivity.
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is recommended in the presence of cholangitis.
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography is useful to look for obstruction of the biliary, pancreatic, or common bile ducts.
COVID-19 infection increases morbidity and mortality for patients with acute pancreatitis.
Clinical rules have been developed and validated that help predict prognosis. The best known are the Ranson, Imrie, and BALI scores.

A simplified 4 variable predictive model has recently been validated (the BALI model). Its overall accuracy, as measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, was better than the Ranson score (0.82 vs 0.75). It is also simpler and the variables can be measured any time during the first 48 hours following admission (see ).
The HAPS (harmless acute pancreatitis score) can identify patients with non-severe pancreatitis.
See for a suggested approach to management of acute pancreatitis.
Enteral nutrition is preferable to parenteral nutrition in patients with acute pancreatitis. B
In acute biliary pancreatitis, early ERCP should be reserved for those with cholangitis. Medical therapy is recommended for patients with biliary pancreatitis without cholangitis. B
Surgery is recommended for those with gallstone pancreatitis, unstable patients with infected necrosis, and persistent pseudocyst. C
Treat pain. Opiates for acute abdominal pain do not affect the ability to diagnose the underlying condition.
Fluid therapy is generally recommended for acute pancreatitis although the evidence for this intervention is poor.
Agressive fluid resuscitation may lead to fluid overload without improvement in pancreatitis outcomes.
Early aggressive intravenous fluid therapy hastens clinical improvement in mild acute pancreatitis.
Lactated ringers are the preferred intravenous fluids for resuscitation as it may decrease systemic inflammation and have better outcomes.
Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended in severe or necrotizing pancreatitis as they have not been shown to improve outcomes.
Infected necrotizing pancreatitis should be treated with antibiotics.
If caused by hypertriglyceridemia, treat to lower level to less than 500 mg/dL.

For infected necrotizing pancreatitis, surgery is indicated if the patient is unstable. For stable patients, antibiotics may be adequate. After 30 days of antibiotics, drainage can be considered endoscopically, radiologically or surgically.

For patients with infected necrotizing pancreatitis, a randomized trial with 104 patients found no difference in outcomes between early catheter drainage within 24 hours or drainage that is delayed until the infected area is encapsulated.
Cholecystectomy should be done during the same admission for acute biliary pancreatitis. Early cholecystectomy shortens hospital length of stay in patients with mild gallstone pancreatitis.
Patients with mild pancreatitis due to gallstones do better with early rather than delayed cholecystecomy (NNT= 16 to prevent recurrent pancreatitis).
Early cholecystectomy improves outcomes following mild gallstone pancreatitis more than delayed surgery.
Necrosectomy or drainage should be reserved for those who have signs of infection and are unstable or have ongoing symptoms.
Two systematic reviews of ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy for acute biliary pancreatitis found that it was associated with fewer complications (NNT = 8) and lower mortality (NNT = 26).
A meta-analysis identified 11 studies of Chinese medicinal herbs for acute pancreatitis. While some reported benefit, they were small, poorly designed, and/or poorly described. C
Probiotics increase mortality in patients with severe pancreatitis (NNT = 11).

A meta-analysis of 6 studies of limited quality found that nasojejunal enteral nutrition in patients with acute pancreatitis results in fewer complications and shorter hospital stays than parenteral nutrition.

A more recent meta-analysis of 5 studies of patients with severe acute pancreatitis found that enteral nutrition was associated with fewer infectious complications (RR = 0.47), fewer pancreatic infections (RR = 0.49), and lower mortality (RR = 0.32).
Early tube feeding (within the first 24 hours) in patients with severe pancreatitis does not improve outcomes compared to on demand feeding.
Plasmapheresis is an option in patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia causing acute pancreatitis, but evidence is limited.
In patients with mild acute pancreatitis a combination of non-opioid pain medication, early ambulation, and patient directed oral intake improves time to refeeding.
Steroids and rituximab are treatment options in autoimmune pancreatitis.
Clinical rules have been developed and validated that help predict prognosis. The best known are the Ranson, Imrie, and BALI scores (see ). B
Severe pancreatitis is also indicated by elevated C-reactive protein, white blood cell count, hematocrit, BUN, and glucose. B

In a cohort of 7456 admissions for an initial diagnosis of acute pancreatitis, readmission occurred in about one-quarter during a median 40-month follow-up, and a diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis was made during that same follow-up period in approximately 10%. Risk factors for recurrence including alcohol as the etiology and tobacco use.
The strongest risk factors for development of chronic pancreatitis after a first episode of acute pancreatitis are recurrent episodes and alcohol as the causative factor.

cell.label: Acute pancreatitis diagnosed: Order CBC, complete metabolic profile, CRP, amylase, lipase
Assess severity using validated clinical rule: (Ranson Rule 137, BALI Rule 350, or Imrie Rule 139 scores).
Basic treatment includes fluid resuscitation, monitoring vital signs, enteral nutrition, and pain relief; nasogastric suction only in presence of ileus. Improving?
Continue supportive care; advance diet as tolerated.

Order contrast CT to rule out cyst, abscess, or other diagnosis; admit to ICU for respiratory and hemodynamic support, enteral nutrition, and management of organ failure; give antibiotics to prevent infection.
Continue antibiotics and supportive care; consider necrosectomy/drainage if unstable or not improving.
Percutaneous drainage or surgical debridement and drainage; continue supportive care.
